text.text: Run the studio from here. The Class schedule is your weekly timetable with each teacher and their pay per class. Students carry their pass, classes left, pack expiry, waiver date and any injuries. Class bookings fill each class; the Dashboard shows failed member payments and packs about to run out.
The passes you sell, their price and how many students hold each.

The weekly timetable. Change a teacher or a time here and every page shows it.

pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the studio runs in this workspace. Share it with the studio manager, the front desk and every teacher.
: memberships, class packs, drop-ins, privates and workshops, with price, what is included, expiry and how many students hold each.
: current pass, classes left, pack expiry, waiver date, injuries and cautions, visits, no-shows and payments.
: the weekly timetable with teacher, time, style, level, room, spots and pay per class.
: who is booked into which class on which day, and whether they came.
: member charges, pack sales, drop-ins, failed charges and refunds.
A class from booking to paid
A student books a class (or walks in). The booking links to the class on the timetable.
At the door, the desk checks them in and updates their pack.
Drop-in and pack payments are taken at the desk; member charges run monthly.
Every morning: Dashboard, failed payments, today's first-timers
Every week: packs expiring in 14 days, waitlists
Every pay period: teacher pay from the bookings
Every season: timetable review from bookings by style
Change the passes, prices and timetable to your own, and delete the sample students once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Injury notes are confidential: teachers read them before class and never mention them in front of others.

When a class is full, add the student as a booking and tell them they are on the waitlist. When someone cancels in time, the first person waiting gets a text and the spot. Classes that fill every week with a waitlist are your signal to add a second time.
Class attendance, payments and pass health.
Students should never be surprised by what their pass allows. Clear, written rules, applied the same way by everyone at the desk, prevent nearly every awkward conversation.
: every group class, billed monthly on the card on file. Can be frozen for up to two months a year (travel, injury). Thirty days' notice to cancel.
: expires 120 days after purchase; can be shared with one family member.
: one class, paid at the door.
: priced and paid separately; members get 10 percent off workshops.
is filled only for passes that expire.

to the number of classes, and
to the purchase date plus the expiry days.
After each class they attend, take one off Classes left.
When one class is left, the student card says

The Dashboard lists packs expiring in the next 14 days. Send a friendly note a week before: "You have two classes left before the 20th." Many studios allow one extension of two weeks on request; decide your rule, write it here, and apply it to everyone.
A freeze needs a request in writing (a text or email is fine) and a restart date. Set the student to
; no charge is taken while frozen.
Cancellations need thirty days' notice; set the student to
Failed card charges show on the Dashboard: contact the student the same day.

Ask for twelve hours' notice to cancel a booked class, so someone on the waitlist can take the spot. A no-show on a pack uses up the class. After three no-shows the card suggests a conversation; most students just need a reminder of the rule.
A student buys a 5-class pack on the 1st. Her card shows 5 classes left and an expiry 60 days out. By the 40th day she has used four; at check-in the desk sees
and mentions that the 10-class pack works out cheaper per class. She buys it before her last class.
Teachers stay where the schedule is predictable and pay is right, on time, every time. Keep the timetable in one place and pay from it.
Every regular class is one row in
: day, start time, style, level, room, spots and teacher.
Build the week around what students actually book. The Dashboard chart shows bookings by style; a class that runs under a third full for six weeks is a candidate to move or change.
Publish the schedule a month ahead and change it at most once a season.
. Common models are a flat rate, a flat rate plus a per-student bonus above a headcount, or a share of the class revenue. Pick one and write it in the teacher's agreement.
At the end of each pay period, filter Class bookings to the period and teacher, count the classes taught, and multiply by the class rate. Add privates and workshops at their agreed share.
Pay on the same day every period.
A teacher who cannot teach finds a sub from the studio's sub list and tells the manager at least 48 hours ahead.
The manager changes the teacher on that day's bookings, not on the timetable.
The sub is paid for the class; the regular teacher is not.
What a good class needs from the teacher
Arrive 15 minutes early; room warm, lights and music set
Ask about injuries and pregnancy; check the student card for
Mark everyone attended or no-show before leaving

At the end of the month the manager filters bookings to Kenji: twelve classes (lunch express and yin), at $40 and $45, plus one private at half the price. The total goes to payroll that afternoon. Yin has averaged 16 of 18 spots, so she adds a second yin class on Sundays next season.
A new teacher assists two classes, then teaches a community class with the owner present, then joins the sub list before getting a regular slot.
The first five minutes in the studio set the tone of the class. A calm, warm, clean room and a friendly desk are worth more than any marketing.
Opening, 30 minutes before the first class
Lights on, heat or air set (hot classes: preheat 45 minutes)
Floors swept, mats and props straightened, blocks and straps in their bins
Check today's bookings and the waitlist; note any first-timers
must be filled before they practice
Greet every student by name. First-timers get a tour: cubbies, bathroom, mats, where to sit.
Pack holders: take one class off
Drop-ins pay at the desk; press
Tell the teacher about first-timers and any new injury notes.
Mark the class done; set anyone booked who did not come to
Wipe down loaner mats with a mat cleaner; air them out
Return props, open windows if the room is stuffy
Five minutes between classes to reset the room before the next group arrives
Every class of the day marked done; payments match the payment list
Heat and lights off, doors locked, alarm set
Lost and found tidied; items older than 30 days donated

A Tuesday evening: the desk sees three first-timers for Power hour. Each signs the waiver, gets a tour and a mat near the front. After class the desk marks the two who did not show, wipes the loaner mats and resets the room for the 7:30 yin class with five minutes to spare.
Know where the first aid kit and the defibrillator are. If a student feels faint, stop them, help them lie down, and call for help if it does not pass in a minute.
